account: In a Nature paper of 27 April 2022, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used a structure-based machine-learning algorithm. The algorithm, an ensemble of three three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, selected stabilizing mutations in a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolase, producing FAST-PETase. They reported that untreated post-consumer PET from 51 different thermoformed products was almost completely degraded within one week at 50 degrees Celsius. The authors report that FAST-PETase “shows superior PET-hydrolytic activity relative to both wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 °C and a range of pH levels.” The researchers then resynthesized PET from the recovered monomers. In a paper of 26 September 2023, Carbios scientists and academic co-authors reported that FAST-PETase converted 18.1 percent of post-consumer PET in 24 hours under larger-scale conditions, against 97.3 percent for the enzyme LCC-ICCG. They concluded that its low rate may not permit use at larger reaction scales. In September 2024 a University of Waterloo group reported that FAST-PETase made by engineered wastewater bacteria degraded about 40 percent of a commercial PET film in four days at 50 degrees Celsius. The group reports that the enzyme also degraded part of a post-consumer PET product. An independent group at Texas A&M University used FAST-PETase together with MHETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst (Environmental Science and Technology Letters, 19 March 2025). The yeast system produced 4.95 mM terephthalic acid from PET film after seven days at 30 degrees Celsius, with no accumulation of MHET intermediates. The authors report complete depolymerization of PET into its monomers. Their reported yield does not establish that the entire starting film was degraded.

ai_role.statement: The machine-learning model chose which mutations to introduce. The designers measured the enzymatic activity experimentally. A separate group at another institution later reproduced it, using FAST-PETase as a component of its own system.

later.note: An independent Texas A&M group adopted FAST-PETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst and reported complete depolymerization of a PET film in seven days.

fields.account: In a Nature paper of 27 April 2022, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used a structure-based machine-learning algorithm. The algorithm, an ensemble of three three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, selected stabilizing mutations in a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolase, producing FAST-PETase. They reported that untreated post-consumer PET from 51 different thermoformed products was almost completely degraded within one week at 50 degrees Celsius. The authors report that FAST-PETase “shows superior PET-hydrolytic activity relative to both wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 °C and a range of pH levels.” The researchers then resynthesized PET from the recovered monomers. In a paper of 26 September 2023, Carbios scientists and academic co-authors reported that FAST-PETase converted 18.1 percent of post-consumer PET in 24 hours under larger-scale conditions, against 97.3 percent for the enzyme LCC-ICCG. They concluded that its low rate may not permit use at larger reaction scales. In September 2024 a University of Waterloo group reported that FAST-PETase made by engineered wastewater bacteria degraded about 40 percent of a commercial PET film in four days at 50 degrees Celsius. The group reports that the enzyme also degraded part of a post-consumer PET product. An independent group at Texas A&M University used FAST-PETase together with MHETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst (Environmental Science and Technology Letters, 19 March 2025). The yeast system produced 4.95 mM terephthalic acid from PET film after seven days at 30 degrees Celsius, with no accumulation of MHET intermediates. The authors report complete depolymerization of PET into its monomers. Their reported yield does not establish that the entire starting film was degraded.

ratings.reason: Independent groups at Texas A&M University and the University of Waterloo reused the enzyme in their own laboratory systems. The sources report bench work and no production deployment.
